title: The Purpose of School Inspection Is What It Does
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau applies systems thinking to school inspection, arguing that its purpose is not what its architects intended but what it actually does -- and what it does is reward the management of appearances over genuine improvement. He draws on the principle that institutions convert aims into incentives, routines, and consequences, often producing outcomes no one designed and no one wants. Just as virtuous policy aims can create vicious incentives, school inspection aims at improvement but creates incentives for compliance theater. The article argues that replacing school leaders is the wrong lever because the same structural pressures remain after the leadership changes. Didau ends by asking what a better inspection system might look like, implying that genuine improvement requires redesigning the incentive structure, not just revising the stated purposes.
points: The purpose of any institution is what it does, not what it says it does: school inspection says it drives improvement but actually rewards the management of appearances, because the incentive structure converts improvement aims into compliance behaviors.

Systems convert aims into incentives, routines, and consequences -- producing outcomes no one designed: an attendance policy can improve numbers while making school feel hostile to vulnerable families.

The root cause of poor school outcomes is rarely leadership incompetence -- most struggling schools are led by people doing their best under punishing conditions; replacing them leaves the same structural pressures intact.
Good intentions are necessary but insufficient: the history of well-intentioned policies shows that virtuous aims regularly create vicious incentives that no one designed and no one can easily undo.

Success and failure in school leadership are always influenced by luck -- punishing the unlucky deters others from taking on the most challenging schools, concentrating disadvantage in the system's hardest cases.
quotes: Just as teachers don't always do what their leaders hope they'll do, neither do schools always behave in ways system leads expect. Although this sounds obvious, we often live our lives pretending otherwise. We write plans, set priorities, clarify expectations and assume our noble intentions will translate smoothly into our desired outcome.

What if the more troubling possibility is also more useful? What if schools are systems that can produce poor outcomes even when most of the people inside them are well-intentioned, hardworking and competent?
Virtuous aims can still create vicious incentives. An attendance policy can improve the numbers while making school feel more hostile to the families most in need of trust.

This is the logic behind school inspection: if a school is underperforming, its leaders must be the problem. Expose them, replace them, and improvement will follow. But this isn't just wrong, it's foolish. Replace the leader and the same pressures remain: recruitment problems, unstable budgets, weak local services, inherited curriculum gaps, hostile accountability.
